I have a confession to make. It’s time I came clean. Slow cinema is pretentious bullshit. I was pretending to like it because I liked how it made me look, how it made me feel more distinguished and sophisticated than others. The truth is, slow cinema is boring. All that talk about “a matrix for time” and “the language of dreams and memory” was really just me being a contrarian poser. My Aftersun review was written by ChatGPT. I rave about Chantal Akerman and Tsai Ming-Liang and Apichatpong Weerasethakul because it earns me woke points to praise a lesbian woman and gay South Asian men. In reality, Uncle Boonmee doesn’t make shit for sense, I slept through Jeanne Dielman all three times, and I only made it through Goodbye, Dragon Inn because I was watching the screening of Dragon Inn playing in the background. Andrei Tarkovsky’s filmography is only good as a sleep aid. My real favorite directors are Taika Waititi, the Daniels, and Steven Spielberg. Honorable mention to my respected peer Wesley Wang. The purpose of art is not, as I have before parroted, to “expand consciousness”. It is to entertain. i did actually catch sátántangó in a theatrical screening today and that was super cool, although i admittedly didn’t love it. there are many things about it that i think are phenomenal, and i certainly understand the praise, but i’m afraid béla tarr’s particular approach to slow cinema doesn’t entirely work for me, at least to the same degree as my aforementioned denounced favs. still undeniably a monument of cinema, very worth a watch. i could be more specific but for now that’s the gist. only other thing i’ll say is, while i’m grateful for the two intermissions we got for the sake of my legs and stomach, this movie definitely works better watched straight through. next time i see it (whenever that is lol) it will ideally be entirely uninterrupted. real rating is four stars. rite of passage 👍

The pinnacle of pretentious bullshit. I wasted my entire Sunday on this shit. Fuck you, Tarr Béla. Fuck you and all your sycophants. The people who love this movie will tell you that it's a revolutionary thing, a deconstruction (or outright rejection) of cinema laden with symbolism, metaphor, and parable. They are EXTREMELY wrong and COPING like a motherfuckers. If you go your entire life hearing "horse shit tastes delicious, when I first ate horse shit it changed my life, horse shit is actually the food of the gods" then when you consume horse shit you are going to search for that brilliance and meaning which simply isn't there and you will find it because you are expecting it. The people who think Sátántangó is one of the greatest films of all time are similarly deluded. To get the obvious out of the way, my issue is not simply that the film is 7.5 hours long. I can absolutely seeing myself loving a movie that long. The issue is that in this prodigious runtime, Tarr accomplishes what most semi-competent directors do in a third of that time. Every scene in Sátántangó is long, every action is filmed in one take along with a hundred other actions, every exterior scene must involve characters walking in wide shots for ten minutes at a time. What does it add to the narrative, to my immersion, to the meaning? Fuck all. There are absolutely reasons to include the mundane in your story, to include scenes where little happens, to let a moment linger. What anyone who's seen three movies before can tell you, though, is that when every scene is like that, it loses all impact. The audience gets bored because they are just watching some morbidly obese alcoholic lie on the floor of his room for five minutes and it means nothing to them. Any piece of media that simulates reality is just that: simulation. When you play a video game, read a book, watch a show, you are not looking to exist in the 1:1 moments of life. Why the fuck would you? When you experience those moments in your own life your mind is usually elsewhere, so why would it be any different when you are being presented the same moments but in an obviously fictional story with fictional characters doing fictional shit that, above all else, is just plain not fucking interesting. Anyway, I know I'm not going to win over any die-hard Tarr fans. All I can do is warn people away from this movie. It is the biggest waste of time movie I've ever seen and it masquerades as meaningful and impactful cinema, a far worse crime.

I really liked this film. Especially the visual concept was overwhelming. Also the narrative approach was really fascinating. The first half was perfect -would have been a 5/5 for me. The second half lost me because it diluted the highly complex character confrontation into a more kafkaesque societal critique which didn’t work as well as the first parts. But it still would have been a very engaging watch with different layers and magnificent filmmaking. I would‘ve loved to appreciate this film even more, wouldn’t there be this one scene in the first third which completely destroys the whole picture. A young girl tortures a cat for about 20 minutes and then kills it. I know that the director has given interviews and tried to explain that they did take care of the animal but it’s really not that convincing. I don’t care if there was a vet on set or that the cat was sedated. You tossed that poor soul around for 15 minutes, the cat had to endure to be stuffed in a bag and then her face was excruciatingly pushed into a bowl full of milk (which contained rat poison in the diegesis but not in the pre-filmic reality so the cat was luckily not killed…) You can see that the animal was stressed and extremely anxious. It is animal abuse. I don’t care what people say to deflect. It is animal abuse! So I don’t know what to think of a film that critiques authorities, societal cruelty and indifference of live when it actually produces the same.

Extending any and every scene does not make it cinema, it just makes it boring. Maybe if there was something to reflect on it would be acceptable, but its just a cat eating for 8 minutes, people walking for 20 minutes, or a guy dancing with a loaf of bread on his head for 15 minutes. This is more like an art project similar to Logistics: long and inconsequential. FUCK YOU, BÉLA TARR, FOR HAVING WASTED 7 HOURS OF MY LIFE.

I have no words. Actually, scratch that. I have a lot of words, just not positive ones. I just spent seven and a half hours watching the cinematic equivalent of a stakeout at the wrong house. No perp, no activity. Just an entire day of staring at an empty house. Who in the hell are films like this made for? Is there anyone out there who actually enjoys this kind of cinema? And I don't mean the pretentious film bros who like everything that's hard to pronounce in English. I mean regular folks who just put something on to entertain themselves. I have no clue what this was about. It's the most aimless, meandering, up its own ass movie I've ever sat through. And I watched it over the course of four days at mostly two hour intervals, because watching this in one sitting will result in a loaded .45 scraping my molars as I launch myself into an end credits sequence of my very own. I think it had something to do with communism. There's a scene that drags on for like 20 minutes of a guy just repeating the word "plodding" in Hungarian well over a hundred times. Other times, we just watch people do yardwork, walk, or stare at each other. And because this is a critically acclaimed global classic, there's yet another scene of animal abuse. I consider my time to be valuable. I hate when my podcast forces me to subject myself to stuff like this. There's no reason this film needs to crest two hours, let alone fucking seven. No point is reasonably made. No characters matter. No plot threads are interesting in any way. I feel like I just lost seven hours at the end of my life that could be spent playing with my future grandkids one last time. Sorry kiddos. Grandpa had to watch Satantango when he was in his 30s, so now he has to die. Of course, if I go to movie hell, I'll just be watching this for eternity.

Consegui meu selo de cinéfilo, pois assistir a 7 horas de um filme húngaro de 1994, em preto e branco, não é para qualquer um. É uma experiência que exige paciência extrema e uma disposição que poucos possuem. "Sátántangó" é frequentemente citado como uma obra-prima do cinema contemplativo, mas é inegável que sua estrutura representa um dos maiores desafios de resistência já propostos ao público. Embora possua virtudes técnicas indiscutíveis e uma composição visual rigorosa, a obra de Béla Tarr peca por uma dilatação temporal extrema que transgride a fronteira entre o artístico e o exaustivo. A lentidão deliberada, aliada à barreira das legendas e à complexidade narrativa, transforma o ato de assistir em uma tarefa hercúlea, onde o tédio inevitável acaba por sabotar a imersão e dispersar a atenção necessária para captar os detalhes mais sutis da trama. As famosas tomadas longas, que se estendem por minutos a fio, podem até possuir qualidades estéticas de planejamento, mas sua repetição sistêmica gera uma estagnação que testa os limites da paciência. É um filme que exige uma força de vontade quase sobre-humana para ser concluído, deixando um questionamento legítimo sobre o propósito de uma narrativa tão arrastada que afasta o espectador em vez de envolvê-lo. No fim das contas, o filme impõe sua estética através da exaustão: é possível reconhecer suas qualidades formais, mas é difícil ignorar que a experiência se torna, para muitos, um exercício de passividade extremamente penoso.

Decided to watch the entire 7-hour and 19-minute runtime in one sitting, and it's certainly an endurance test. First off, it is a well-crafted film, with the striking black-and-white cinematography being the standout. The extremely slow-moving narrative has intention behind it, to further immerse the viewer in the characters' lives and worldviews, leaving time to reflect within each frame. This does enhance the film's bleak tone and atmosphere, which are strong. Its themes and messages are evident throughout, but they could have been just as, if not more, effectively conveyed without the absurd runtime. For more than half of the film, essentially nothing of substance is taking place, which, in its defence, enhances the feeling of monotony and dullness which these characters are experiencing; apart from that, it's incredibly tedious to sit through and only diminished my engagement. There are points where the slow-moving, quiet, lingering shots are appropriate, but the majority are unjustifiably long to the point where no greater effect is accomplished. It is certainly self-indulgent. On a character level, nobody is particularly interesting or likable. It's quite a cold and distant film that's devoid of emotion, which may be the point, but as a viewing experience, it is unrewarding. The performances are sufficient, although somewhat stiff. Despite occasional thought-provoking lines, much of the dialogue is abnormally paced, run-on, and unengaging. The standout is the cinematography, which is fantastic. It creates an immersive, dark atmosphere that delivers countless striking frames within the dirty, gloomy, and rainy setting of the Hungarian countryside. The camerawork is impressively controlled and highly intentional, with smooth, flowing long takes. The tracking shots are especially great. Béla Tarr 's direction is good, and he deserves respect for his ambition and uniqueness. Not to say that there aren't interesting aspects, as certain areas of the film are, but out of the immense runtime, it isn't a good ratio. The pacing, while deliberate, is horrible, and many shots are bafflingly overlong to the point where it's an insult to your time commitment. I was hoping to like this, but I ultimately found no enjoyment in it. It's hard to believe that a substantial number of these 5-star ratings aren't conformity or pretense. But I'm sure some people genuinely like it, which I appreciate. Other films with this slow-moving style have succinctly conveyed their themes in a much more engaging, impactful manner, such as An Elephant Sitting Still ( Béla Tarr was the mentor of the director, Hu Bo ) and Eureka , to name a few.

English: László Krasznahorkai’s original novel has 232 pages. Breath in. This movie is a 432 minutes endurance test. Breath out. If you’ve actually endured it yourself in one sitting like me and my friends you probably need some time to inhale it, this pedantic egotrip fever dream. When you look at other cinematic titans of extreme length, whether it’s the historical grandeur of Sergei Bondarchuk’s seven-hour “War and Peace” or the crushing, slow burn domestic dread of Chantal Akerman's “Jeanne Dielman”; the massive runtime actually serves a purpose. In those films, the scale builds a world or mirrors a lifetime; every heavy minute earns its keep. Sátántangó, by contrast, feels like a psychological hostage situation, Stockholm syndrome really. Cows, curtains, mud, rain, unbroken 10 minutes of it’s stillness doesn’t add artistic depth or value it’s just a trap, maybe even a social experiment to see if they could coerce the audience into nodding along. And they do!!!! If not, they seem uncultured, cinephile’s worst nightmare. I felt as if my patience was being insulted at times, there is after all a difference between building atmosphere and indulging in cinematic masturbation. It’s a cult film that actually has it’s own cult of blind lovers who will sing endless praises, even after experiencing first hand hours of numbness. They will even say it’s a “meditative movie”, my dearest friend… I invite you to actually try and meditate. It makes me remember when Yoko and John Lennon lost their child, they released an experimental track “Two Minutes Silence” that, as you can guess, has two minutes of nothing and then a heart beat. It uses the absence of sound to signify the devastating void and loss of their pregnancy. It was called avant-garde. I would say in this case there’s is a lot of “something in nothing”. Sátántangó has a hell of “nothing in something”. I had some respect for the cinematography in it self, even if it was, undoubtedly dull, it was undeniably well shot, plain pretty. That all kind of vanished the second the infamous cat scene began. No amount of dark moody cinematography can wash out the taste of a director using cheap shock tactics to simulate profundity. It was animal abuse. It was cruelty. And the fact that it was played out under the guise of “high art” is vile. I despised the scene. The two stars rating I gave stand for the company I had with me while surviving this monolithic slog. The movie is aggressively self-serious and yet, it is an accidental comedy. We spent some portion of it laughing. It wrapped it up to be somewhat of a friend group rite of passage. If you stripped away the director's self-indulgence, there was actually a stellar two-hour movie fighting to get out of this text. As it stands, the film is most definitely a trap. Our watch was worth it, we will always share the memory of surviving a cinematic fever dream together. We will, unfortunately, always have Sátántangó. Português: O livro original de László Krasznahorkai tem 232 páginas. Inspira. Esse filme é um teste de resistência de 432 minutos. Expira. Se tu realmente aguentou assistir isso em uma sentada, como meus amigos e eu, provavelmente precisa de um tempinho para ‘digerir’ esse delírio febril de uma egotrip pedante. Quando você olha para outros titãs cinematográficos extremamente longos, seja o grandioso histórico de 7h de Sergei Bondarchuk “Guerra e Paz” ou o slowburn terror doméstico de Chantal Akerman “Jeanne Dielman”; o tempo de tela massivo serve a um propósito. Nesses filmes tem uma baita construção de mundo ou um literal espelho de uma vida inteira; cada minuto pesado justifica sua existência. Sátántangó parece uma situação de refém, nível Síndrome de Estocolmo. Vacas, cortinas, lama, chuva... dez minutos ininterruptos dessa imobilidade não adicionam profundidade ou valor artístico. É apenas uma armadilha, talvez até um experimento social pra ver se conseguiriam coagir o público a concordar cegamente a qualquer palhaçada que o Tarr colocasse ali. E as pessoas concordam!!!! Se não o fizerem, parecem incultas: o pior pesadelo do cinéfilo. Senti como se a minha paciência estivesse sendo insultada às vezes. Afinal, há uma diferença entre construir atmosfera e se render à masturbação cinematográfica. É um filme cult que realmente tem seu próprio culto de amantes cegos, que vão cantar louvores intermináveis mesmo depois de vivenciarem, em primeira mão, horas de puro entorpecimento. Vão vir com um papo de “filme meditativo”, eu humildemente os convido a meditar de verdade. Isso me faz lembrar de quando a Yoko e John Lennon perderam um bebê e lançaram a faixa experimental  “Two Minutes Silence” que, como você pode adivinhar, tem dois minutos de nada e depois um batimento cardíaco. Eles usam a ausência de som para significar o vazio devastador e a perda da gravidez. Foi chamada até de música de vanguarda. Eu diria que, nesse caso, há “algo no nada”. Já Sátántangó tem “nada em algo”. Eu tinha algum respeito pela fotografia em si; mesmo sendo, sem dúvida, monótona, era inegavelmente bem filmada, simplesmente bonita. Tudo isso meio que desapareceu no segundo em que a infame cena do gato começou. Nenhuma quantidade de fotografia sombria e melancólica consegue apagar o gosto de um diretor usando táticas baratas de choque para simular profundidade. Foi abuso animal. Foi crueldade. E o fato de isso ter sido encenado sob a pretensa de “alta arte” é vil. Eu desprezei aquela cena. As duas estrelas vão para a companhia que tive enquanto sobrevivia a esse massacre monolítico. O filme é agressivamente solene e, no entanto, é uma comédia acidental. Passamos uma boa parte do tempo rindo. Acabou se tornando uma espécie de rito de passagem para o nosso grupo de amigos. Se você retirasse o egocentrismo do diretor, provavelmente haveria um filme genial de duas horas lutando para sair dali. Do jeito que ele realmente se apresenta, o filme é definitivamente uma armadilha. A nossa sessão valeu a pena e sempre compartilharemos a memória de termos sobrevivido juntos a um delírio febril cinematográfico. Nós vamos, infelizmente, sempre ter Sátántangó.

My understanding of slow cinema is that it's slow to give you time to contemplate the ideas in the film — to give the viewer a sort of meditative experience. But when there doesn't seem much depth to contemplate, sometimes the slow pace just feels dull or tedious or annoying. Never-ending scenes of drunken dancing or people walking or a drunk yelling wore out their welcome. I couldn't stand the cat sequence. Even if the cat was safely drugged and the yowling was from a sound effects library, as Tarr has said, it seemed an awful ordeal to put a live animal through. Horrible. And even if they swapped out the live cat at certain rough moments — in fact, even if the cat was never harmed at all — it was distressing and distracting enough to take me completely out of the movie. I wasn't thinking about the character hurting the cat, I was thinking about the actor and the filmmaker. Sátántangó lost me there, in chapter 4 or 5 of 12. I had been okay with the film until then. Following that chapter with the interminable drunken yelling and dancing sequences kept me pretty sour on the rest of the film. The story was extremely thin, the nonlinear structure was slightly interesting but ultimately felt pointless, and I didn't care about any of the characters. If there's a point to be made about someone tricking people, it feels undercooked and unconnected to the first few chapters. I don't mind slow or long, and I love some films that are both (some Tarkovsky, for example), but this material didn't feel like it earned its length or pace to me. The cinematography and sound design were excellent. And I loved the textures of the locations/sets — all the crumbling walls, etc. I saw the 4k restoration from 2019 in the theater as part of Bleak Week 2026 at AFI Silver. After the screening, they gave us each a cinephile certificate for braving the entire seven hours, which was a fun idea. I wish I loved the movie like most people who sit through it do. I liked Werckmeister Harmonies okay. I don't know if I'll bother with another Tarr film.

I typically respond to Béla Tarr, Tarkovsky and Angelopoulos--the heavyweights of ‘Slow Cinema’-- like Michael Scott does to Toby Flenderson. I wish they weren’t the way they are, and I hate everything about who they choose to be. I say this because I think I share a fundamental comedy-writer’s sensibility, a fundamentally different worldview than these cinematic sloths. When I stare into the existential void, I see the same abyss they do. I too am a true misanthrope, and believe in the fundamental folly of my fellow man, and I fully understand the inevitability of entropic decay and the looming maw of death. But when I stare into the abyss, I choose to laugh at it. The work of humanity is to fight against chaos, not sit in paralyzed fear over it. I refuse to wallow the way that Tarr does, because that way there be dragons—dragons I vanquished years ago, and ones which I do not want to manifest to fight again. I am aware that much of the structure of this film is in service of the novel Sátántangó, which apparently also suffocates the reader with dense, unbroken paragraphs that loop back on themselves, but if this is a miserable thing in service of a miserable thing, that doesn’t make any of it any easier to swallow. The Letterboxd average for this film suggests that most people rate this film 5 stars, and I must say it bluntly: their subjective opinion is objectively wrong. This film is an asshole of a thing, self-pitying, stubbornly stupid, masturbatory, and excruciatingly boring, more fascinated with emptiness and entropy than an emo teenager reading Tolstoy in their depression nest. The only nice thing I will say about this film is that within this gaping 7 hour maw, there are plenty of opportunities to take a break. However, I’d especially encourage people to wait until someone starts walking. Anytime you see anyone walking, feel free to leave the room, take a pee, maybe even go make a sandwich, fold some laundry, whatever because they will STILL be walking when you get back, having gone nowhere in particular. Stuff not happening happens a lot; the stuff that does happen is mostly unpleasant. Slow cinema as a style does not bother me. Normally, slow cinema exists to mimic the phenomenology of a stagnant, looping, dwelling thought or obsession. It is meant to indicate inactivity of thought and action. It is also, as far as I can tell, almost always a cinematic device meant to artistically represent someone–the writer or director or even just a character–who is unable to think themselves out of some rut. When I like it, I like it. But when I don’t like it, I like to hold someone responsible. Here, I’m saying it reflects the stunted, miserable, nihilistic worldview of Béla Tarr. He is sad, depressed, and completely obsessed with the concept of overwhelming entropy, and so we must endure a seven-hour cold-plunge into this icy state of being. Ironically, the very fact that Tarr obsessed over and meticulously organized an ordered treatise on entropy shows the hypocrisy and failure in his thinking, but the man himself just can’t get out of his own way, and so we must be punished to seven fucking hours of his miserable self-pitying and depression. I think I could almost enjoy this if Tarr openly admitted he was fucking with us at the end, that he admitted the ideology of the film was obviously full of shit, and the whole thing was a cruel joke played on snooty, self-flagellating cinephiles, a meta-commentary on the plenary indulgences of difficult cinema that the bourgeois festival circuit endures for cultural capital. That would display a brilliant, transgressive sense of humor that Tarr, a miserable miserablist, simply doesn’t have in him. If you picture this film ending not as it does–with someone boarding themselves up into literal darkness–but with a Looney Tunes “That’s All Folks” title card, and Tarr himself walking out on screen, breaking the 4th wall, and flipping us off, I’d appreciate what he was doing. But Tarr doesn’t have a drop of humor to him. He has no spark of joy or life. Viktor Frankl would say he has lost his Will to Meaning.Tarr asks us, in a dead-serious tone, to approach his nihilism, his futility, and his depression with the same severity he does. And I refuse. I get that it’s supposed to be an allegory of the socioeconomic stagnation of post-Soviet Hungary, but you can’t discuss socioeconomics with allegory and mood. This isn’t an operant thought or ideology. It gets us nowhere. All we are doing is dwelling, wallowing, visually and sonically fetishizing the idea of feeling miserable inside of chaos. I find it very hard to respect an ideology that is fundamentally based on bad weather, shitty architecture, and some miserable director who refuses to go to therapy. I frequently wonder why I, or anyone else, would willingly subject themselves to this sort of cinematic-waterboarding. Maybe it’s the inherent agony of how slow this is, downregulating our receptors. Maybe it’s like a silent meditation retreat for city people, forcing us to sit in boredom so that the real world feels profoundly sharpened after, a sort of digital-detox. But I live on a mountain in Vermont, so, this was just boring for boring, I’m not a shaky-brained broccoli-hair with no attention span, I sit and write for 6 hours a day. The correct way to turn a short story into a Tolstoy length novel is to add new stories and characters, not to paraphrase every single sentence a thousand times. This film could easily have been told in two hours. Instead every scene is slowed down on purpose. You get cows mooing for 10 minutes. Two men walking in silence for 10 minutes. A drunk repeating the same line for 10 minutes. A bar dance where nothing happens for 20 minutes. An old man taking five seconds just to say a single word. At some point it just becomes unintentionally hilarious. I’ve never liked the idea of being avant-garde just for the sake of it. Experimental techniques are fine, but they should actually serve the story. I enjoyed the dreams in 8½, the non-linear structure of The Mirror, the shifting identities in Fanny and Alexander, and the surreal elements of Bunuel, because they all deepen the way the story is told. This one, however, feels like an intentional joke meant to waste the audience’s time. The plot is quite simple. A con man who looks like Jesus working with the police manipulates a group of depressed villagers. That’s not a complex story to tell. So what does a 20-minute bar dance actually add to it? What's the point? That said, the cinematography is quite beautiful. That’s the main reason I’m giving it two stars instead of one.

My first Tarr film and maybe not the best one to get me acquainted with his work, I tackled this behemoth over three consecutive evenings as I don't think I'm physically capable of sitting through 439 minutes of sparse Hungarian dialogue accompanied by a lack of music in one go. I'm afraid I may have to hand in my cinephile card as this just wasn't for me. I don't mind a leisurely paced film but when a maximum of 2 hours of content is stretched out to fill 7.5 hours I think it's going too far. Some nice black and white cinematography but I don't think I need at least five minutes per shot to appreciate it (which is a shame as I usually like a long shot but not to the point where it becomes tedious). The story was okay and I enjoyed seeing different people's perspectives of the same events overlapping each other but I struggled with the lack of subject matter for the runtime. The extended animal cruelty scenes of a young girl torturing a cat are horrible to watch and whatever Tarr has said about the safe practises they used on set that cat still looked distressed throughout and it made me genuinely angry and quite upset watching it. I think I can officially say that 'slow cinema' is probably my least favourite film genre. They are supposed to be contemplative but I don't think I've seen one that I haven't fallen asleep watching (I've tried quite a few now including Yi Yi , Memoria , Uncle Boonmee and most of Andrei Tarkovsky's filmography and I think I've nodded off in every single one). I wish I enjoyed these films as much as most other cinephiles do but I find them tiresome and a challenge to get through and not in the least bit rewarding.

I’ll just say it: this movie is too fucking long. I’m not even going to claim it could be cut down to one hour without harming the story—but the truth is that some parts feel less like art and more like a kind of perverse exhibitionism. A ten-minute shot of cows moving from point A to point B? Fine by me. But shots that have no clear beginning, middle, or end, and that stretch on for as long as analogue film physically allows, just feel unbearably pretentious. I’m 100% certain I could trim an hour off this movie and no one would notice. That said, there’s a lot I genuinely liked. I love the way the film is shot, and how certain compositions repeat like a visual refrain. Despite everything I’ve written above, I also love the way some shots are allowed to unfold—the scene with Irimiás and his group waiting for the fog to lift, the second shot of the film where we wait for the sun to fully rise, and so on. Still, when it was over, it felt like I’d spent seven hours watching a film whose main message is simply that life is torture. And unlike The Turin Horse , I felt absolutely no motivation to search for any deeper meaning.

Overly long, pessimistic nonsense. This one sentence is more than enough to rate this film and the source material as well. This work is a supposed love letter from Tarr to his great friend, Laszlo Krasznahorkai, who managed to come up with the original novel. Tarr was always very observant of Krasznahorkai' body of work, the two frequently collaborated. The major flaw of this movie is that Tarr decided to adapt one of the most boring and uninspired works of Hungarian literature. Krasznahorkai' personal philosophy is devoid of external references to our shared experiences, his overly pessimistic and oftentimes nihilistic outlook never managed to capture the historical and geographical context of everyday Hungarian life. His novel, and Tarr' subsequent movie thus feel alien and completely isolated, they only exist and thrive within their perverted and twisted minds. The characters are grossly oversimplified and generalized versions of everyday folk people, the plot and narrative paint a harsh, hopeless picture, but ultimately fail to capture any semblence of reality. The core premise of the movie can be interesting for outside observers, people who never familiarised themselves with the end of the century sociopolitical climate in Hungary, but the message gets lost for native viewers. People suffer just to suffer, struggle just to struggle. Misery can be captivating, but these two can never portray it adequately, which is an overarching critique of 20th century Hungarian literature and filmmaking in general. Watch this mess at your own risk, but I'd suggest everyone to simply read the novel, that alone is a mind-numbingly painful intellectual excercise. The runtime serves as ample justification for the worst people you know to call anyone who dislikes this work a brainless maggot, further fueling their pretentious nature.

Bleak Week - 1 Screening at the Aero Theater Bela Tarr is one of those rare filmmakers that has inspired distinctly volatile reactions out of me. I've felt utter despair, frustration, bliss, and serenity within the methodical saga's he crafts. I'll admit that most of them don't fully work as cohesive pieces for me. They have their peaks and valleys. This is the first one that *mostly worked for me. Shocking considering this is the dreaded seven hour behemoth that's existed as this abstract terror in the back of my head. For most of this I was genuinely enthralled. Still, there are some issues I do take from it. I can only really quantify it by breaking it into two camps. Pros - His intersection between incredible lighting, blocking, period accurate set design, and framing is operating with gravitas here. The stark reality of an economically ravaged Hungary post Soviet Union has never been more pungent in it's visual hopelessness. There are so many sequences that still cause me to ruminate in my mind. The lingering pan of a man's binoculars being one that permeates my daily thoughts. It's truly transformative visual storytelling that lands when it's employed at it's most meaningful. I also felt this one carried his best performances out of the actors. They all has a truthfulness to their portrayal of desperately seeking an ascension from the squalor you reside in. That fanatical hope that boils within to hopefully find a new home where the suffering stops. Capturing how this community comes together even at their worst to dance and throttle themselves against the tide of nihilism. Something that is viciously shredded with the arrival of Irimas. The "man in black". An economic opportunist whose goal is to exploit the village labor in the decade of "new opportunities". The manipulation involving his character abusing the trust of the village was heartbreaking and it resulted in my first Bela Tarr experience where it succeeded in making me upset. The final third of this was satisfying and felt complete in ways his others faltered. Cons - While I do think the emotional payoffs allotted by the acting and visual work are exceptional. It doesn't lend enough credence for me to ignore some of it's flaws. The pacing is sluggish, and at worst lends to a dull experience sometimes. So much of the middle section in this film dragged it's feet and didn't feel substantive enough to allow those creative decisions to feel meaningful for me. That's also my consistent grievance with his work. The visual language and acting certainly compounds impact to the subject matter in his stories. There's just not enough meat to his writing to make me connect with his characters beyond a symbolic level. They feel like instruments for him to ramble through rather than individuals with their own compelling arcs. That can work with specific instances in the film. But, at points it does just devolve into lengthy composition for the sake of it. If it wasn't so repetitive in structure then I'd probably be more forgiving. It just wears itself thin rather than  resembling any sort of cathartic accomplishment with finishing it. I also have a huge issue with his use of violence. Whereas Haneke can make me feel tremendously startled with suffering I just feel empty and frustrated with Tarr. I think this is derived from the fact that Haneke feels purposeful in how he inflicts it on others. He doesn't forget these are people at the core and the suffering carries the weight of the universe on it for that reason. Tarr feels volatile for the sake of it. Torturing a cat is not symbolic for a communities spiritual dysfunction. I think it's just icky and I hate it. I don't find unstimulated animal abuse ethical or warranted no matter how imperative it seemed to him as a filmmaker. Luckily, I only had the displeasure of seeing the cat's head dunked into the bowl after stepping outside the theater for a brief respite. He can say there was a vet present on set all he wants. I saw that cat's eyes on the screen. I can't ignore it. Otherwise, glad I can finally excise this one from my celluloid to-do list.

I need an injection of Subway Surfers STAT Really split on Satantango. For the prologue, first two chapters, and several after, I was super drawn in by the deliberate shots, great imagery, and dialogue. But as it went on, I honestly just got fed up with the length and pace of everything. I could not stand 1 hour of "Old alcoholic Hungarian gasps and stutters into the mic" in chapter 3 and in Part 2, when I got to minute 10 of the accordion playing the same two bars during the dance sequence I started losing my mind. And I knew I still had three hours ahead of me! I also just bristle against how this is structured in terms of themes. Even with my issues with the first two parts, I love how it focuses in on the Void of this society. There's no comfort, no community, no solidarity. Everyone has their knives out, looking for a chance to satisfy their selfish urges at the cost of others, animals, or their own health. But then having all of that come up against a promise from Irimias that he'll make a community only for that to collapse so quickly without seeing the potential for anything more just felt so abrupt. Bleak Week: Year 5 For years, Satantango had existed in my mind more as a challenge than a movie. It had built up this almost mythical reputation: the seven-hour runtime, the impossibly long takes, the reputation for being one of the bleakest movies ever made. So when the opportunity finally came to watch it in a theater, there was no way I was going to pass it up. After spending an entire day with it, I can safely say that it is one of the most challenging cinematic experiences I’ve ever had. The runtime is obviously part of that challenge, but it’s also the way Béla Tarr asks you to experience time itself. Scenes stretch on far beyond what most filmmakers would allow. Characters wander through mud, rain, abandoned buildings, and endless disappointment while the camera patiently observes. It’s not a movie you watch so much as a movie you endure, and to Tarr’s credit, there are stretches where that approach is genuinely mesmerizing. What I found interesting was how deeply the collapse of communism hangs over the movie without constantly announcing itself. The people at the center of the story feel stranded in the aftermath of a system that promised something better and delivered very little. Everyone seems trapped between a dead past and an uncertain future. The village itself feels like a state of mind, populated by people desperately searching for purpose, direction, or someone to tell them what comes next. That’s where the movie’s idea of the false prophet becomes so powerful. When people are abandoned, isolated, and stripped of hope, they become vulnerable to anyone who promises meaning. The movie understands that desperation can make even the most unbelievable promises sound reasonable. It becomes less about whether someone is telling the truth and more about how badly people need something to believe in. For about the first three hours, I was completely locked in. The atmosphere is incredible. The black-and-white cinematography is stunning, the long takes create a hypnotic rhythm, and the sense of decay is so overwhelming that it almost becomes tangible. There’s a weight to every frame that few filmmakers can achieve. However, somewhere around the midpoint, I found myself slowly disconnecting from the experience. What initially felt immersive started feeling repetitive. The deliberate pacing that had drawn me in began to test my patience rather than deepen my engagement. I understand why Tarr structures the movie the way he does, and intellectually I can appreciate it, but emotionally I started feeling the length more than the ideas. Instead of becoming more profound as it went on, it began to feel like it was reiterating points I had already understood hours earlier. That’s ultimately where I landed with Satantango . I admire it far more than I actually like it. There are images and ideas that will stay with me for a very long time, and I completely understand why many people consider it one of the greatest movies ever made. If I’m being honest with myself, though, I don’t see myself ever watching it again. I’ve felt this way about much of Béla Tarr’s work. I keep wanting his filmography to resonate with me more than they actually do because I can clearly see the artistry on display. His filmmaking is uncompromising, ambitious, and unlike almost anything else. At some point, however, I have to admit that he may simply not be a filmmaker for me, and that’s okay. If nothing else, Satantango reaffirmed that. For those who do connect with Tarr’s wavelength, this is probably a masterpiece. For me, it was an admirable but exhausting experience, and if you do decide to watch it, prepare yourself. This is not a movie for the weak. Few movies stare into hopelessness with this much patience, and even fewer ask you to sit with that bleakness for seven and a half hours.

I undertook the seven hour challenge of Satantango for my 4000th movie. While the film was painful to watch, it had alot of intelligence and a fascinating, layered message about nihilism, economic depression and stagnation. Satantango was about society in decay and the stupid human animal clawing for light as the sun dims forever. Satantango follows the occupants of a miserable, rural Hungarian village. Hope is fading fast and the villagers begin to conspire against eachother. A charismatic leader emerges in the enigmatic Irimiás. Irimiás' kind words and hopeful demeanor make him a beacon the villagers can't help but to follow mindlessly. After the apparent suicide of a local girl, Irimiás convinces the people to abandon their village and scatter. He promises that they will come together again someday but in his report to local authorities, it is revealed that he had nothing but hate for them. Satantango scrutinizes the harsh realities of economic disenfranchisement and the hopelessness of choosing between fight or flight. It's a damned if you do, damned if you don't situation. The villagers can remain in their homes to die alone and cold or they can follow the pied piper into a world they can't begin to understand. The doctor represents stagnation; boarding yourself into your home and never budging from what you know. Irimiás represents foolish ambition; rushing off into the wilderness, buying dynamite, changing the plan and ultimately sending everyone to different places. The main current of Satantango is despair; the human animal pushed to the brink and the scant, heinous outcomes available from there. It takes two to Satantango, if you will and the film does great at illustrating the haunting dualities of hopelessness. Do you flee or rot? Live in pain or die? Do you wish foolishly or despair knowingly. The death of the little girl affirms the very worst of the situation. She abuses and kills her cat just as the world abuses and kills her. Even the deceitful Irimiás can't help but to point to the town's negligence as the cause of her passing. European art films often use children as symbols of hope; the prospect of a new generation unburdened by the agonies being explored. Satantango's choice to kill her affirms that the sun will not rise for these people and their nihilistic inaction will be their ultimate undoing. The money tree was an interesting symbol; a foolish little game for the child to make her think that prosperity was a possibility. She is distraught at it being uprooted even though it was never going to yield anything anyway. So too the villagers behave when Irimiás is late to his 6:00am rendezvous. They squabble and fight because their false prophet is missing; as if he was going to be able to help them anyway. The money tree represented the placebo of hope and how, worthless though it may be, uprooting hope will always outrage the truly helpless. Fascinating movie with lots of great ideas. I took issue with its execution though, particularly in its animal abuse and time wasting. I don't think Satantango was elevated by its runtime. It made me sit with its desolate ideas for seven hours, which was effective in conveying the necessary emotions but... not needed. Satantango tells a two hour story over the course of seven and while that choice may have had meaning, it was also super inconvenient. Satantango had some great, artful messaging but also some very effective visuals. The composition was subtle but the levels, shadows and perspectives were simply marvelous. The film had some unforgettable tracking shots and some great compositional nuance. There was alot to appreciate visually, which only slightly compensated for the infuriating, samey soundtrack and audio design. Satantango is considered by some to be essential but I don't know anybody I would condemn to watch this movie. It's only something for lunatics like me who can look past the fog of its duration and derive some meaning from it all. The hard part about Satantango is that... it's inordinately melancholic. It really makes you sit with the dread, moreso than any film I've ever seen. It ends with the old, drunk doctor boarding himself into his shack, leaving him in darkness as he soliloquizes about his miserable fate. Its length and its tone make it a difficult film to appreciate but its ambition is admirable. Satantango is one of the most relentlessly dark films to ever exist and I admire that tremendously. It did well in passing its agonies onto me. Maybe there's something to be related to the long, painful experience of Satantango and the long, painful experience of watching 4000 movies over the course of my life... The definition of a challenging watch, not least because it was an all-nighter at the Prince Charles Cinema ending at 7 in the morning. Bleak, long and uncompromising. Auteurship distilled - no one is telling this guy to trim down a scene in the edit suite. Paths stretch into the horizon, pushing us forwards; doors shut in the camera’s face, abruptly locking us out. In some ways this mirrored my experience of watching the film. In the second act, there is a very long scene of unsimulated animal cruelty which took me out of the film’s carefully created world and instead (unfortunately, I felt) pushed my attention elsewhere, outside the film and towards the other side of the cameras. Therein lies my frustration: Tarr’s stark landscapes, ultra-long takes and handheld tracking shots create a world that beckons inwards, but moments like this - and also when some scenes run and repeat themselves past the point of absurdity - jettisoned me outwards and alienated me. Which is not what you want when it’s 4am and you’re reminded that you’ve got a sore back, caffeine sweats and you’re fighting to keep your eyes open.

Both novel and film arrange their chapters along the tango’s rhythm of advance and retreat. But the “steps” feel mechanical, rigid—and perhaps this is precisely what the title names: Satan’s tango. The Doctor’s viewpoint functions as panorama, yet moves like someone with a stiff neck: there is only one direction available. Yet does this trainlike motion ever actually carry us into the interior of a single character? Estike may be the exception. In the film’s long and notorious cat-torment sequence, we glimpse a character with genuine desire—which may be why she earns the film’s most powerful tracking shot. But this too makes me angry. It is no way to film an animal like that.

A morosidade do movimento e a ideia de repetição como que "aligeiram" um filme de reputada duração, mas ficamos ainda assim a pensar por que será afinal este filme assim "tão longo" ou, pelo menos, muito mais longo do que o habitual. Uma interrogação estúpida, é certo, mas um juízo ao qual o filme parece querer prestar-se. De uma cinematografia virtuosa, Tarr emprega o plano-sequência de forma belíssima, seja através de um quadro fixo, seja por travellings onde todas as peças parecem cair no seu devido lugar. O humor do filme, naquele ermo tão lamacento, é bem ajustado, não demasiado sarcástico, nem particularmente interessado em fazer cair as suas personagens no ridículo. Uma sátira de um fim dos tempos, esse tango com Satanás, a momentos tão triste e tão decadente, sempre conduzido pelo inexorável interesse no valor formal do plano. Se nos lembra Tarkovski, surge-nos como algo de muito mais focado na sua própria importância. Um pouco de ambição nunca fez mal a ninguém, sobretudo quando acompanhada de tamanho rigor, mas Satantango parece-nos hoje algo indissociável da sua própria história, e nisso algo de mais impressionante do que essencialmente estimulante.

For å holde meg i stil med både filmen og boken velger jeg å skrive denne anmeldelsen uten bruk av linjeskift. Dette er første gang jeg har sett en så lang film. Et riktig heldagsprosjekt som startet i kø på Cinemateket rundt 14:00 og endte etter klokken hadde bikket 22, og hodet var utkjørt. Åpningsscenen i filmen er en ~10 minutters lang scene med kuer som går rundt på en gjørmete gårdsplass og gjør som kuer gjør. Det er uventet, og kanskje på grensen til provoserende å ha så lange scener i en film når man er vant til å se tradisjonelle spillefilmer hvor hvert sekund i en scene på en måte må rettferdiggjøre sin eksistens i filmen. Satantango oppleves nesten som en protest mot dette. Videre i filmen blir publikum eksponert for flere slike scener. Når scenene varer i over 5 minutter med ting som rytmisk monoton gange, litt rar tangodansing, eller mennesker som ligger på gulvet og sover, blir man overrasket når scenen plutselig skifter. Mildt komiske eller pinlige scener blir forsterket når de bare varer og varer, og det blir etter hvert absurd. Etter hvert som noen av scenene drar på, glir blikket over bildet på jakt etter noe - helt til det er umulig å finne flere detaljer. Man går gjerne over til å tenke på middagsplaner for uken, eller at man angrer på at man tok morgenflyet fra Bergen og bare sov 6 timer akkurat denne dagen. At denne søvnigheten man kjenner på sikkert ikke er på grunn av filmen, men bare det at man har hatt en lang dag. Jeg innser etter hvert at jeg ikke kan skylde på dette; det er mange andre i salen som også tilsynelatende sliter med tretthet, og noen sover skamløst i stolene. Man flytter seg i stolen, lener seg litt fram, så tilbake. Forsøker å stramme leggmusklene. Lener seg fram igjen. Ruller litt på skuldrene, for så å lene seg tilbake igjen. Alt for å våkne til litt, men så fokuserer man igjen på skjermen, og det er vanskelig å si om scenen av en jente som løper over en åker i det hele tatt har endret seg. Man lukker øynene litt lenge og merker søvnen komme krypende, før man tar seg i det og nok en gang skifter positur. En scene i filmen er spesielt forstyrrende. Den involverer dyreplaging og en katt. Per forsikret meg i ettertid om at internett forsikret ham om at det var filmtriks. Håper endelig det. Filmen er utrolig gjørmete. Den er delt inn i tre akter, og når man kommer ut i pausen er det uvant at det ikke er gjørme overalt. Så inn igjen. Mer gjørme. Ubehagelige lyder fra en alkoholisert og utflytende doktor. Lyder som får det til å høres ut som bare det å eksistere er en strevsom affære. Det er på mange måter en dystopisk film, og handler i bunn og grunn om oppløsningen av et kollektivbruk etter Sovjets fall. Det eneste som kan minne om en lykkelig slutt ved denne filmen er vel egentlig at den er ferdig, og at man ikke lenger er fastlåst i en stol. Filmen er forresten i svart-hvitt. Etter seks timer med dette begynner hjernen å legge inn farger der det ikke er noen. Luen til den ene karakteren syntes jeg liksom var litt gul. For øvrig er boken kun i overkant av 300 sider. Dette betyr at fortellingen muligens kan formidles like raskt i begge medier. Jeg slet litt med å skulle gi denne filmen en karakter. Til visse tider synes jeg filmen er dårlig og blir bare frustrert, mens andre ting oppleves veldig flotte, og jeg tenker at det er gjerne et poeng bak lengden på filmen. Etter en uke betenkningstid har jeg imidlertid klart å lande på en slags karakter, men å skulle sette et nummer på noe som dette blir litt som å putte julemiddagen i en blender og forvente at mottakeren får inntrykk av om middagen var god eller dårlig. Uansett, anbefaler å se filmen hvis du først er lang-film-curious. Hvis du kjenner deg selv så godt at du vet at dette blir for mye, hold deg unna!

Pues hoy me levanté to pronto y me dije: es hoy, hoy es el día que me veo Satantango como que me llamo richi. Dicho esto agarré mi vaso de leche matutino y me puse con ello. He de decir que mi intención siempre fue vérmelo del tirón, pero un wachin tiene deberes como wachin que es visitar a su wela y me ha partido el visionado. Pero bueno igualmente lo he podido ver en el mismo día. Primero, no son 7 horas de historia sin parar, está separado por capítulos no autoconclusivos pero sí interconectados. Lo cual no era lo que me esperaba pero como me gustan ese formato de historias pues no hay mal que por bien no venga. Ahora bien, la historia no es nada impresionante, siento que es una historia que ya se ha contado y probablemente sea así, su toque reside más en el costumbrismo y el tomarse las cosas a su tiempo. El narrador interviene pocas veces pero cuando lo hace es muy bueno, mis ejemplos favoritos es su monólogo sobre la libertad y el orden o sobre la niña tumbada en el cesped. De esta última escena hay algo que me gustaría destacar de la película, si bien todo apunta a que es una película depresiva (desde el lugar donde viven hasta el comportamiento de los propios habitantes) se puede notar ciertos atisbos de esperanza. No hay tanto fatalismo como uno piensa, sino que existe un sentimiento de tranquilidad, de que todo ocurre por algo y las cosas están conectadas por algo. Y me encanta esto, me encanta porque a pesar de que en esta película se muestran un montón de cosas horribles del ser humano siempre reside ese deseo de que existe una salida. Y es una gran representación del mundo real, de que pasan cosas horribles todo el rato, que parece que estamos sumidos en las profundidades más oscuras de nuestro planeta, pero siempre hay un algo que te hace decir: calma, hay una vía. Hay pequeños detalles bonitos del mundo escondidos pero joder que si merecen la pena, definitivamente mi escena favorita. Hay una escena que detesto y probablemente sea consenso general y es la del gato, horriblemente alargada. Una cosa es provocar una reacción pero otra muy distinta estrujar esa reacción de tí. No me ha gustado nada. Ale pues ya tengo mi insignia de haber visto la peli de 7 horas. Realmente no tengo problema viéndolo, no me incomodan los planos contemplativos, solo que algunas veces lo siento exagerado. Entiendes sus costumbres su forma de moverse y de vivir pero ya está, tristemente no puedo conectar emocionalmente con ellos a través del costumbrismo. No tengo pueblo, no conozco a la gente de mi barrio y definitivamente no puedo sentirme identificado con ninguno de los personajes. Tal vez me falta madurar, me falta vivir para poder apreciar la lentitud de las cosas o pertenezco a una generación tan edulcorada que empatizar con una obra de esta lentitud me es una tarea imposible de realizar al completo. Por eso no me ha gustado, no ha echo ese click en mi cerebro que me hace decirme a mi mismo "esta es mi mierda". Siento que Jeanne Dielman por otro lado sí puede hacerlo, me pica la curiosidad esa película. La historia no me parece sorprendente, y no por su falta de grandilocuencia, simplemente no me ha maravillado. Eso sí, soy capaz de respetar la obra que es, y no es para nada una obra más, es una propuesta interesante y necesaria para avanazar en los límites de lo que es posible hacer con el cine. Lo que no voy a hacer es ponerle mayor nota de la que he sentido para autoconvencerme que cada minuto de estas 7 horas han valido la pena, es una peli como cualquier otra y no por ser larga es mejor. After owning a collection of Bela Tarr’s films for over 18 months, I have only now watched my first of his films, deciding to subject myself to the director’s most well known work, this seven-hour, 12-minute behemoth of an experience. To say having the ability to boast of having watched a seven hour black and white film about a Hungarian commune at various social interactions within the next few months did not cross my mind beforehand would be wholly dishonest, however now having completed such, I do strongly maintain that there is far more to this work than merely its fruits as a pretentious conversational topic. Satantango is a portrayal of a very consuming sense of hopelessness, that of a minute community in complete isolation. To refer to it as bleak would naturally be a thorough understatement, with the characters within carrying the heavy shackles of being abandoned and forgotten by a system nearing total ruin. It is towards the goal of building an understanding of these ideas that the only very-slightly-longer-than-average runtime acts as a crucial element. Having thought through this, it is really only a ‘bleak’ film that could truly benefit from such length. A seven hour rom-com would beat even the most soppy spectator into mental decay. A seven hour action film would have entirely used up the allure of explosions and choreographed fight scenes by the fourth hour at the very latest. I’m sure my point here is sufficiently illustrated. It is the ability of this rare cinematic element to construct a sensation of living alongside its characters through heavy, extended exposure to any and all aspects of their lives, rather than existing solely as a half-enthusiastic witness, that suits such a bleak atmosphere tremendously. This consideration does, however, come with a caveat. Even in the midst of bleak filmmaking, such length works to a far greater extent if it remains a unique feature. It seems this is something Tarr was wise to recognise, given none of his other works are even close to as prolonged, preventing a sense of stylistic fatigue. As such, Satantango is a film I would argue to be experimental in a sense, its merits being not insignificantly because of the fact that it’s very existence almost discourages the making of something too similar for fear of being overshadowed as an uninspired copy. Perhaps I have spent too significant a portion of this review aiming to justify the runtime, but I do wholly insist that it functions as nothing short of vital in delivering the final atmospheric result, regardless of the notion that any individual scene could be removed with seemingly minimal loss (we could have trimmed that dance scene down just a tad though). Above all else, Satantango is a numbingly bleak film, bleak in the miserable lives it contains, those tormented by a false saviour, and numbing in the incredibly extensive exposure to this bleakness that it subjects its brave viewers to.

A typical film being 1 to 3 hours is not by accident, 3 hours in my opinion is about the max amount of time someone can comfortably pay attention to something, before biological directives start to seriously interfere with the experience.  So to first address the elephant in the room of the film's length of being 7 hours and 19 minutes, makes it difficult to share this experience or recommend this to others.  That being said for the people who have sat through this entire film, you in my view are among the elite and you have been rewarded by experiencing a film this glorious.  I suspect, however, the length itself deters many who would dislike this film, and this has likely inflated the rating here on letterbox. But its not all inflated. Satantango has some serious positive qualities to me, I love large ensemble casts interacting each other, with long pans and still shots. The film is quiet meditative and oppressive atmosphere permeates through out the entire thing. The gloomy atmosphere is bolstered by the endless rain, but they must have not been able to coordinate filming on many actual rainy days, as the angle of the rain makes it clear the characters are just being sprayed with water from an off screen sprinkler of some sort.  This would be fine in 99% of films, but given the long scenes, I am talking 5-10 minute scenes of walking through the rain, the cheapness of the effect becomes too obvious to ignore.  There is also several continuity errors with people walking through the rain, enter a door, then the next seen their hair is completely dry. The long takes also suffer, especially egregious is, arguably most famous scene, where the villagers are crowded around someone who definitely, by plot, is not supposed to be breathing but plainly is. I can imagine there would be several ways to mitigate this. This is a common pattern throughout the whole film, that the long takes, take priority over believability of effects. Something is lost here. I should state for the record, that I have not read the book, though I am quite interested to after watching this.  With some cursory research it does seem that the book laid more foundation for the source of Irimias power and influence over the villagers.  The film despite its length fails to do so, which in the beginning develops intrigue, which is not later satisfied through the narrative.  That being said it does sort of work in a quasi-mystical sense, that the villagers just simply believe in this man despite all evidence informing them not to. Not to say that the plot itself, is poor, in a lot of ways this is among the best I have seen. The slow unfolding of the story, and then to rewatch the same scenes from a different perspective is brilliant.  This is a masterpiece of storytelling, with some minor foundation issues, that are hardly an issue if you can just accept that Irimias has power. The same suspended disbelief request is made in famous films like The Godfather series, and Casablanca come to mind. The film does depict a cat being tortured and killed. I generally do not like films that employ actually harming animals as an effect. See Milo and Otis, or Andrei Rublev.  However, after some research the cat dying was simulated, and the cries it makes out were dubbed in. So this is not even close to the same degree as either of the films I mentioned.  The scene is crushing, but does so within the bounds of animal ethics. Philosophically, is where this film shines. Which seems to be the focus on most reviews here on Letterbox. I will not contradict any of them. I think it reveals the darker sides of human nature, and makes a strong argument regarding serious flaws in humanity. This is not a hopeful message, but I do not believe every film needs to be hopeful.  But if you are not ready for a 7 hour contemplation on the darker side of humanity, then I would not recommend this. But as I said before, I generally would not recommend this film, despite me thinking that its great. The film is its own reward for those willing to commit to it.

wonderfully purgatorial experience watching this movie in the Astor, each of its three sections themselves as long as a (long) movie. truly felt my attention, my alertness and just the basic needs of my body as tangible components of the art that slowly frayed over the course of the afternoon/evening, whether i was rationing out ten kernels of popcorn per shot during the middle half or lapsing into drowsiness as the characters struggled to do the same at the decrepit mansion Irimias leads them to. beyond this meta-experience, does the length serve the movie? i think so. within each long, trudging sequence, each action the characters take - from dancing to dictation - is often repeated ad nauseam, until all meaning or intentionality fades away. it is as if the movie is populated with automata, or more appropriately, ghosts, drinking themselves into a stupor even though they have long since drowned in cobwebs. one moment towards the end that really stuck with me is right after Irimias has given the villagers their new orders they just stand there vacantly in eerie stillness for just a bit too long. they are dancers for whom the music - either their own petty squabbles or Irimias' hypnotic tune - has stopped and who are incapable of moving on their own. this feeling extends to all the characters to varying extents, no-one feels truly alive. even Irimias, who seems like the exception to this rule, is later revealed to be a mere pawn himself, as his verve and personality is literally editorialised out of the record by his superiors. the world of Satantango is not a hell, as its title might suggest, but a purgatory for which time has begun to lose its meaning. events layer over eachother and stretch beyond comprehension whilst the past lingers in a far-off belltower. i think its important then, that the audience feels time too, and by god did I feel time watching this. with all that being said though, i feel like all the formal choices that allow Béla Tarr to tell this story in a 7.5 hour film end up just reflecting the natural strengths of the story's original novelistic form. this movie is a remarkably faithful adaptation, but that closeness to the source material - in form if not content - only makes me more interested in revisiting the novel and its greater sense of interiority. still, this is a masterpiece on so many levels that I can't help but appreciate it. I spent several weeks finishing this seven-and-a-half-hour hypnotic, slow-moving, but brilliant adaptation of the novel Satantango. There is a lot to admire about Béla Tarr’s approach and composition. This is not a film you simply watch. You slowly surrender to its rhythm. Tarr layers the film almost as one continuous circle, with events repeating and overlapping, moving forward and backward almost like the steps of a tango. People seem incapable of escaping the desperate time and place in which they live. They move, they wait, they drink, they scheme, they hope, but somehow they always end up back where they started. Tarr sets all of this against a desolate landscape that seems almost incapable of allowing the people within it to escape. The mud, the rain, the empty buildings, the endless roads all become part of the story. His use of black-and-white gives the film even more character. The slow shots, the slow pans, the gradual movements of the camera, the continuous shots of cows, pigs, people walking through the rain. Everything is deliberate. At seven and a half hours, Satantango demands patience, but its length is also essential to what Tarr is doing. You begin to experience time the way these characters experience it. You feel the waiting, repetition, boredom, desperation, and occasional hope. The slowness stops feeling like a filmmaking technique and becomes the atmosphere of the film itself. It is an extraordinary choice by Tarr, and somehow it works. By the end, the repetition, the landscape, the black-and-white photography, and those endlessly patient shots have created something completely hypnotic. You do not simply understand the world of Satantango. For seven and a half hours, you live inside it.

When one has almost an entire month off work as they contemplate their next steps while in the midst of a semi middle-life crisis as they watch the country in which they live fall into an economic stupor that may never end while they are feeling the effects of a cold given to them by their young son who is about to turn two which film should one watch sat on their sofa on a Tuesday afternoon as the endless rain tap tap taps on the window? Why of course. It's Béla Tarr's 7 hour 20 minute magnum opus on depression and despair and bleak, bleak alcoholism. And my isolation and sense of distance from anything and anyone at the moment meant that I had no one to talk me out of it. Yay!!! And yes. I watched it virtually in one sitting bar a few short breaks. Satantango is something quite unlike anything I've ever seen. Slow cinema defined. Surrealism defined. European horror defined. Endurance cinema distilled and bottled for consumption like the Doctor's pálinka. There are shots so long you question whether your YouTube feed has frozen, but you don't want to get up and check it because that might cause you to check out, to give up. White flag raised and torn asunder by the wind and rain and circling trash. There are monologues and single character portraits that are films in their own right. There is animal torture and bizarre dancing and drunken spouting about "plodding, plodding, plodding I plod", trips out into armageddon to get more booze, three bean soup and speeches over the corpse of a dead girl as a phantasmagorical fog that just might be her spirit dances above her final resting place. You might argue this is a referendum on communism. But it could just as easily be one on Hungarian fruit brandy. Or the petty greed of your fellow man and lady. Or mud. Or cow shit. There's a scene, which I believe to be the film's most famous, in which our cast of rotten, boozy, filthy farm folk dance a bizarre tango for what feels like forever, as in the eternal forever that hell might turn out to be. David Lynch would very much have approved. It's cinema as broken record. It's also the most accurate depiction of the most miserable depths life can take us to I've perhaps ever seen put on film. And when it's all said and done the spiders come out to have their fun. The score is stunning. Either a booming rotten synth that feels like the soundtrack to that endless hell we might find ourselves in post-death I mentioned upstairs or just a complete lack of any sound at all. The photography even more so. Black and white has never looked like this. Tarr takes his camera through beer crates and the sides of characters faces and just lets it sit, lets it do its magic. And then there is the tedium. Satantango pulls us into the monotony of these people's lives and then asks the question; is yours any better? Perhaps. Perhaps not. Perhaps we just need to laugh at it all. Capitalism. Communism. Greed. Despair. Elation. Sexual desire. No desire. Booze. Cigarettes. Rat poison. Dirt. Rain. A swirling cloud of trash and cardboard that hits us in the arse as we walk to nowhere. Doing Satan's tango.

Oh Satantango, how do you even begin to rate and review this movie? I don't think its unreasonable to assume that essentially every person that watches Satantango does so because of its length, I know I did. Whether that be for dork bragging rights, or as a personal challenge of willpower, or as morbid curiosity to test the limits of your own suffering to feel the slightest sense of meaning in an uncaring void of a universe. Satantango is 7 hours long and you don't need anyone to tell you that that is too lengthy of a fucking runtime for a movie. The narrative in this movie is emotionally deep, but it is not so uniquely profound as to warrant 7 hours by itself. If you are however willing to set the length, the one thing most people know the movie for, aside, you are still left with a great film in its own right. So no, its not a bad movie that's good because its 7 hours long, its a great movie but it would be better trimmed. From the get-go, Bela Tarr chucks you into purgatory, disguised as the Hungarian countryside, and leaves you to absorb all its pessimism, apathy, vapidness, crypticity and weltschmerz. He treats you to grimly gorgeous shots, even if in a sluggishly slowly paced, non-linear structure, presents a set of deeply evocative but stoic characters and lets you marinate in that dark totality for 7 hours as the philosophical web gets strewn around you. The hypnotic immersion into the dark world and the characters is the movie's greatest achievement, and it does so better than any movie I have ever seen. I guess mostly because it takes its sweet ass time introducing you to them. I think the story is done weirdly, and is my main critique of the film. I'm fine with a movie that doesn't have a traditional story arc, but this felt like it was both trying not to and to have one near the end. I think as a mood and atmosphere piece, a gallery of shot composition, a theatre of very realistic performances and a testament to the fact that people will watch your movie just because its 7 hours long and has a cool name, Satantango is impeccable. I cannot however in good conscience give it a flawless 5, because of the aforementioned story's clumsiness and the sheer stupid needlessness of its length. Sure, Satantango couldn't be what it is if it had a blockbuster runtime, but I can't imagine why the movie HAS to be longer than 5 hours at most. There is much that could be said about the narrative and what it represents, much of which I don't yet have access to because I haven't sat with the movie long enough to develop those thoughts. All in all, while it is not perfect, I found it a phenomenal experience still and will see it the next time its showing in a theatre.
